parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Torque (TQ)**
> 
> Torque (TQ) services and repairs cars in country H. It began in 2010 as a single garage owned by Elif, whose objective at the time was simply to earn enough to keep the business open.
> 
> By 2018 TQ was well established and Elif set a new objective of opening ten garages within five years. TQ now has twelve.
> 
> Electric vehicles have grown quickly in country H.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Electric vehicles in country H**
> 
> | Share of new cars sold that were electric, 2018 (%) | 4 |
> |---|---|
> | Share of new cars sold that were electric, 2025 (%) | 31 |
> | TQ mechanics qualified to service electric vehicles (%) | 15 |
> 
> Electric vehicles need less routine servicing than petrol cars, and most of TQ's mechanics are not yet qualified to work on them. Elif's objective for the next three years is to have every mechanic trained to service electric vehicles.

Explain **one** reason why TQ's objectives have changed over time.
parts.solution_md:
One reason is that TQ's circumstances have changed as the business has developed **[1]**. In 2010 Elif's objective was survival, because a new garage with no reputation could easily fail; once TQ was established she was able to aim for growth instead, reaching twelve garages **[1]**. The objective has changed again because the market has moved, as electric vehicles rose from 4% to 31% of new car sales while only 15% of TQ's mechanics can service them, making training staff more urgent than opening further garages **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Objectives change as a business moves through different stages of its development, and as market conditions, technology, competition or regulation change around it
> 
> AO2
> 
> - In 2010 TQ was a single new garage with no reputation, so survival was the realistic objective; a new business that pursues rapid growth before it has customers is likely to fail
> - By 2018 TQ was established and had the reputation and cash flow to support expansion, so growth to ten garages became an achievable aim
> - Electric vehicles have risen from 4% to 31% of new car sales and need less routine servicing, so TQ's existing repair work will decline regardless of how many garages it operates
> - Only 15% of TQ's mechanics can service electric vehicles, so training has become more urgent than expansion - opening further garages staffed by mechanics unable to service a third of new cars would not help TQ
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks why something has changed, your answer must show both the before and the after. Naming only the current objective describes the situation rather than explaining the change, so use the dates and figures in the case to show what shifted and what caused it.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Quill (QL)**
> 
> Quill (QL) runs private language schools in country J. It teaches English and Mandarin to adults and employs 60 teachers across four schools.
> 
> QL's owner, Dieter, has told staff that his objective is "to grow the business and improve teaching quality". Managers at each school have interpreted this differently. One has spent money on new classroom equipment, another has reduced class sizes, and a third has advertised heavily for new students.
> 
> At a recent meeting, Dieter's finance manager suggested replacing this with a SMART objective: to increase student numbers from 900 to 1,100 by the end of next year, while keeping the proportion of students who pass their final examination above 85%.

Explain **one** benefit to QL of setting SMART objectives.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that a SMART objective tells everyone exactly what QL is trying to achieve **[1]**. At present Dieter's aim to "grow the business and improve teaching quality" has been understood differently by each school manager, so one has bought equipment while another has advertised **[1]**. Replacing it with a target of 1,100 students and an 85% pass rate would give all four schools the same measurable goal, so their spending and effort pull in the same direction instead of against each other **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - SMART objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-limited, making clear exactly what must be achieved and by when
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Dieter's current aim has been interpreted differently by each of the four school managers, so a specific target removes that ambiguity and aligns their decisions
> - A measurable target of 1,100 students lets QL check progress during the year rather than discovering at the end that the aim was missed
> - Setting a deadline of the end of next year creates urgency, so managers act now instead of treating growth as something to address eventually
> - Including the 85% pass rate stops managers reaching the student target by lowering standards, since both parts of the objective must be met together
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common weakness is to write out what SMART stands for and stop there. Listing the acronym is knowledge, not explanation - the marks come from showing what one of those features actually does for this business. Pick the letter that matters most here and develop that one.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'social enterprise'.
parts.solution_md:
A social enterprise is a business that trades in order to achieve social or environmental aims **[1]**, reinvesting most of its profit into those aims rather than paying it to owners **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A business that exists to achieve social or environmental objectives, funding them through trading income rather than donations
> - An organisation that sells goods or services and reinvests the majority of its surplus into its social purpose instead of distributing it to shareholders
> - A business whose main aim is to benefit society or the environment, with profit treated as a means to that end rather than as the end itself

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is tempting to answer a Define question by naming an example you have learned. An example on its own earns nothing here - the marks are for stating what the term means. Give the meaning first, and add an example only once you have already made both marking points.

parts.problem_md: Discuss why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective.
parts.solution_md:
One reason shareholders of a plc might not support CSR is that it increases costs without directly increasing profit **[K]**. Shareholders invest in a plc mainly to receive dividends, which depend on the business making a profit. CSR activities - such as paying workers more than the legal minimum or reducing pollution at extra cost - use up money that could otherwise be paid to shareholders as dividends **[An]**. Many shareholders, especially large investment funds **[Ap]**, are focused purely on financial returns and will oppose anything that reduces profit without a clear financial benefit in return **[An]**

Shareholders in a plc also tend to think short term **[K] **because they can sell their shares quickly if the business underperforms. The benefits of CSR, such as a better reputation and greater customer loyalty, can take several years to improve profits. A shareholder who plans to sell their shares within the next couple of years **[Ap]** is unlikely to support spending money now on CSR programmes that may only pay off long after they have sold up **[An]**

However, not all shareholders think this way **[E]**. A growing number of investors specifically choose to invest in businesses with strong CSR records **[Ap]**, and they recognise that poor CSR can damage a brand and reduce the value of their shares **[An]**. Overall, shareholder opposition to CSR is most likely when investors are focused on short-term profits **[E]**. If a business can show that CSR will improve profits in the long run, even profit-focused shareholders may change their minds **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 9-12 | - Effective evaluation of why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective |
> | **3** | 7-8 | - Limited evaluation of why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective |
> | **2** | 3-6 | - Analysis and application of why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective. |
> | **1** | 1-2 | - Knowledge and understanding of shareholders / public limited companies / CSR / business objectives |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> Why shareholders might not support CSR
> 
> - Shareholders in a plc primarily invest to earn dividends and capital growth, both of which depend on profit. CSR activities - such as paying above-minimum wages, donating to community projects, or investing in cleaner production methods - increase costs without directly generating revenue, reducing profit margins and the dividends available to shareholders
> - Many shareholders, particularly institutional investors managing pension or savings funds, have a short-term investment outlook and measure success by near-term financial returns. The benefits of CSR - improved reputation, greater brand loyalty, reduced regulatory risk - may take years to generate financial gains, making CSR a poor use of resources in the eyes of a shareholder who may sell their shares within two or three years
> - Some shareholders hold the view that the purpose of a business is to generate profit, and that social good is the responsibility of governments rather than companies. From this perspective, CSR represents an inappropriate use of shareholder funds
> - Shareholders may also feel that legal compliance and basic ethical behaviour are sufficient, without the additional cost and management time required for a formal CSR programme
> 
> Why some shareholders might support CSR — evaluation
> 
> - Not all shareholders oppose CSR. The growth of ESG (environmental, social and governance) investing means an increasing number of shareholders actively seek businesses with strong CSR credentials, particularly long-term institutional investors and ethical investment funds
> - Poor CSR can generate damaging press coverage, consumer boycotts, or regulatory action - all of which destroy shareholder value in ways that far outweigh the short-term cost savings of ignoring social responsibility
> - The extent of shareholder opposition depends on the composition of the shareholder base. A plc with a high proportion of short-term, profit-focused institutional investors is more likely to face resistance to CSR than one whose shareholders take a longer-term view of value creation
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
‘Ethics should always influence the human resource management (HRM) activities of a mining business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
The strongest reason ethics should always influence HRM in a mining business is health and safety **[K]**. Mining is one of the most dangerous industries in the world - workers face risks including underground collapse, flooding and toxic gas **[Ap]**. Ethical HRM requires rigorous safety training, proper protective equipment, and clear safety procedures for all employees. Without this, accidents are more likely, and in mining they can be fatal. A business that ignores safety ethics not only harms its workers but risks legal action, government investigation, and reputational damage that could threaten the entire operation **[An]**

Ethical HRM is also important in how mining businesses recruit and manage workers **[K]**. Mines are often in low-income areas where workers have few alternatives **[Ap]**, making exploitation easier. Unethical practices, such as below-minimum wages or unsafe conditions, may reduce costs in the short term but damage morale and increase labour turnover, reducing productivity. Fair pay and transparent dismissal procedures build a more stable and motivated workforce **[An]**

However, "always" is a demanding standard. Fully ethical HRM - better equipment, higher wages, more training - increases costs significantly **[K]**. In an industry where international buyers demand low raw material prices **[Ap]**, ethical businesses can be undercut by rivals in countries with weaker labour laws. If costs become too high and the business closes, the resulting job losses are themselves harmful to workers **[An]**

Overall, I largely agree with the view. Health and safety ethics should always apply **[E]**. No financial saving justifies workers dying or being seriously injured, and the legal and reputational consequences of ignoring safety are too severe **[E]**. Other ethical standards, such as fair pay and working conditions, are important but may be more constrained by competitive pressures. Mining businesses that commit to ethical HRM tend to be more sustainable in the long run - a safer, better-treated workforce is also a more productive one **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
>

> | **5** | 17-20 | - Effective evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a mine if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **4** | 15-16 | - Limited evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of mission statements, strategy and/or tactics |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> **Arguments that ethics should always influence HRM in a mining business**
> 
> - Mining is one of the most dangerous industries in the world. Workers face risks including underground collapse, flooding, toxic gas and heavy machinery. Ethical HRM requires rigorous safety training, protective equipment and clear safety procedures for all employees. Without this, accidents are more likely and in mining they can be fatal. A business that ignores safety ethics faces legal action, government investigation and severe reputational damage, all of which threaten the long-term survival of the business
> - Mines are often located in low-income regions where workers have few employment alternatives, making exploitation easier. Unethical HRM practices - such as paying below the minimum wage, using zero-hours contracts, or demanding excessive overtime - reduce short-term costs but damage morale and increase labour turnover. A demotivated, unsafe workforce is less productive and more likely to make costly mistakes. Ethical treatment, fair pay, and clear dismissal procedures build a more stable and committed workforce.
> - Poor workforce planning in a mining business can lead to understaffing, overworking employees, and increased rates of accidents and absenteeism. Ethical workforce planning ensures the business has sufficient trained workers for each role, protecting both safety and productivity
> - Management that communicates openly and involves workers in decisions improves trust and reduces the risk of industrial disputes - which can be extremely costly in an industry where stopping production even briefly has major financial consequences
> 
> **Arguments against "always" - challenges and limits**
> 
> - Fully ethical HRM significantly increases costs - better safety equipment, higher wages, more training, and better working conditions all reduce profit margins. In a globally competitive raw materials market, businesses in countries with stricter ethical standards may be undercut by rivals in countries with weaker labour laws and less enforcement
> - If ethical HRM costs make the business uncompetitive and it is forced to close, the resulting job losses could be argued to cause more harm to workers than the original ethical compromises - a difficult trade-off with no simple answer
> - The extent to which a mining business can afford to be fully ethical may depend on its size and profitability. A large, profitable multinational can absorb higher ethical costs more easily than a small mining operation in a developing economy
> - In some countries, governments are unwilling to enforce ethical standards in mining because of the tax revenues and employment the industry provides, reducing external pressure on businesses to act ethically
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - The word "always" is key. Health and safety ethics should always apply - the human cost of ignoring them is too great and the legal and reputational consequences too severe. No short-term saving on safety equipment or training is worth the risk of worker deaths or serious injuries
> - Other ethical standards - such as fair wages and working conditions - are important but may be more constrained by competitive and financial pressures. The degree to which these can be applied may depend on the country of operation and the regulatory environment
> - The strongest argument for ethics "always" influencing HRM is the long-term commercial one: safer, better-treated workers are more productive, less likely to leave, and less likely to cause costly accidents. Ethical HRM is therefore not just a moral obligation - it is sound business practice
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

parts.problem_md: Evaluate the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business.
parts.solution_md:
There is a strong argument that a mission statement is only valuable if it genuinely influences how a bank operates. A bank's strategy covers long-term decisions such as which markets to enter and how to manage risk **[K] [Ap]**. Tactics are the day-to-day departmental decisions - such as lending policy and customer service standards - that support this strategy **[K] [Ap]**. If a mission statement shapes neither, it is just a slogan. Many banks produce statements so vague that they provide no practical guidance. A mission statement that changes nothing adds cost without adding value** [An]**

However, mission statements also have external value beyond strategy and tactics. They communicate the bank's values to customers, investors and regulators **[K] [Ap]**, making it more accountable to stakeholders. After the 2008 financial crisis, many banks were criticised for abandoning their stated values **[Ap]**, causing serious reputational damage. A clear mission statement gives stakeholders a standard to hold the bank to, and that external accountability can indirectly shape behaviour even without formal strategic influence **[An]**

Mission statements can also support recruitment and employee motivation **[K]**. Staff who believe in the purpose of their organisation tend to be more engaged and productive. A bank committed to ethical lending may attract employees who share those values, improving morale and reducing staff turnover without the mission statement needing to directly dictate specific tactical decisions **[An]**

Overall, the view is largely correct - the primary value of a mission statement lies in whether it genuinely shapes how the bank behaves **[E]**. A vague statement that changes nothing is of little practical worth. However, its external impact on customer trust and stakeholder accountability means it retains some value even without direct strategic influence **[E]**. The most important test is whether the bank actually lives by its mission. If it does, the statement adds real value; if it does not, it becomes little more than a public relations exercise **[E]**

> | **4** | 15-16 | - Limited evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of mission statements, strategiy and/or tactics |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> Arguments that mission statements are only important if they influence strategy and tactics
> 
> - A mission statement that does not change how the bank actually operates is essentially just a slogan. If it does not shape the bank's long-term strategy - such as which markets to enter, how to manage risk, or what products to develop - it adds cost without adding value. Many banks produce statements so vague ("we put customers first", "we deliver excellence") that they provide no practical guidance and have no measurable effect on decisions
> - Banks are primarily driven by the objective of profit maximisation. If the mission statement conflicts with or simply exists alongside this goal without influencing it, senior managers are likely to ignore it when making real strategic decisions, rendering it meaningless
> - A rigid mission statement could actually harm the bank by locking it into a fixed direction and preventing it from responding to new market opportunities or changes in the economic environment, reducing strategic flexibility rather than improving it
> 
> Arguments that mission statements have value beyond direct strategic influence
> 
> - Mission statements communicate a bank's values externally to customers, investors and regulators. After the 2008 financial crisis, banks that abandoned their stated values faced severe reputational damage. A published mission statement makes a bank accountable to its stakeholders - this external pressure can indirectly shape behaviour even without the statement being embedded in formal strategy
> - A well-crafted mission statement can improve employee motivation and support recruitment, particularly of staff who share the bank's stated values. Employees who believe in the purpose of their organisation tend to be more engaged and productive, reducing labour turnover and improving service quality - benefits that do not require the statement to dictate specific tactical decisions
> - Mission statements can also reassure investors and regulators that the bank has a clear ethical framework, which may reduce scrutiny and the cost of compliance over time
> 
> Evaluation
> 
> - The view is largely correct. The primary value of a mission statement lies in whether it genuinely influences the bank's behaviour. A statement that changes nothing is of limited practical worth, regardless of how well-worded it is
> - However, its external value in building customer trust and stakeholder accountability means it is not entirely worthless even if internal strategy is mainly profit-driven. The two are connected: a credible mission statement can attract customers and investors in ways that ultimately do affect strategy
> - The key judgement is whether the mission statement is genuine or just a PR exercise. If the bank actually lives by it, the statement delivers value both internally and externally. If it does not, it risks damaging credibility when the gap between stated values and actual behaviour becomes apparent
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **UPlane Components (UC) **
> 
> UC is a private limited company providing engine parts for commercial aircraft. It uses batch production in factory A and flow production in factory B. As part of UC’s commitment to corporate social responsibility (CSR), it provides a training scheme for the long-term unemployed, based in factory A.
> 
> UC’s products are sold to aircraft engine manufacturers. Demand for aircraft engines has increased by 45% over recent years. The aircraft engine manufacturers want inventory just when needed and are demanding a reduction in prices.
> 
> In 2017, UC opened factory B which is 5km away from factory A. Factory B has a high level of automation, resulting in low unit costs for the parts produced there. Production is capital intensive. UC has a plan to automate factory A. The production workers are not happy about this proposal and have asked for more details. The workers’ representatives have asked for a meeting with the human resource manager.
> 
> In December 2019 a fault was discovered in one of the engine components supplied by UC and produced in factory A. UC had to recall 2000 parts at a cost of \$200000. This has had an impact on part of its triple bottom line and UC is unlikely to meet its targets. Table 1.1 shows some financial data for UC.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Financial data for UC**
> 
> |   | **Year ending 30 November 2019 (\$m)** | **Year ending 30 November 2020 (\$m forecast)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Revenue | 5.8 | 6.4 |
> | Cost of sales | 2.3 | 3.4 |
> | Expenses | 1.3 | 1.6 |
> | Cost of recall | - | 0.2 |
> 
> Amjit, the human resource manager, believes that the fault was caused by the negligence of Jack, one of the production supervisors. Jack claims that he was made to work overtime to try and meet production targets. This caused him to become tired and make a mistake in one batch of parts. Amjit wants to dismiss Jack.

Explain the term ‘triple bottom line’.
parts.solution_md:
The triple bottom line is a framework that measures business performance **[1]** across three areas: people (the social impact on employees and communities), planet (the environmental impact of operations) and profit (financial performance) **[1]**. For UC, the recall of faulty components would damage all three,  harming its reputation with stakeholders, potentially wasting materials and reducing its profit **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - People - the social impact of a business on its employees, local communities and other stakeholders
> - Planet - the environmental impact of the business's operations, including waste, pollution and resource use
> - Profit - the financial performance of the business, measured through revenue, costs and profitability
> 
> AO2
> 
> - UC's training scheme for the long-term unemployed demonstrates its commitment to the people element of its triple bottom line
> - The recall of 2000 faulty components generated waste and may have increased UC's environmental impact, damaging its planet performance
> - The \$200,000 cost of the recall will reduce UC's profit in 2020, directly affecting the financial element of its triple bottom line
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problem_md: Analyse why mission statements are important to many businesses.
parts.solution_md:
One reason mission statements are important is that they communicate the overall purpose and core values of a business to both internal and external stakeholders **[K]**. Internally, a mission statement provides a strategic backdrop against which managers can set objectives and make decisions. When all departments understand what the business ultimately stands for, their activities are more likely to be consistent and aligned**[An]**. For example, a business with a quality-focused mission will recognise that cutting costs in ways that compromise standards directly contradicts its purpose **[An]**. This reduces the risk of conflicting decisions across the organisation and ensures day-to-day operations support the business's long-term direction **[An]**

Mission statements can also motivate employees by giving them a shared sense of purpose beyond simply earning a wage **[K]**. When employees identify with the values expressed in a mission statement, they are more likely to feel engaged and committed to the success of the business **[An]**. This can reduce labour turnover, lower recruitment and training costs, and improve productivity **[An]**. A business that clearly communicates its purpose - for example, a commitment to sustainability or innovation - may also find it easier to attract like-minded candidates during recruitment, further strengthening its workforce over time **[An]**

Internally, it provides a strategic backdrop against which managers can set objectives and make decisions, ensuring that activities across different departments are consistent and aligned with the business's long-term direction
> - By clearly defining what the business stands for, a mission statement helps managers avoid decisions that contradict the business's stated purpose — for example, a business with a quality-focused mission will recognise that cutting costs in ways that compromise standards is inconsistent with its values
> - Mission statements can motivate employees by giving them a shared sense of purpose beyond simply earning a wage. > - However, mission statements have significant limitations. parts.problem_md: Analyse **two** reasons why a business should set SMART objectives.
parts.solution_md:
One reason a business should set SMART objectives is that time-specific targets give employees a clear deadline to work towards **[K]**, allowing them to plan and organise their work more effectively. For example, a target to 'reduce operating costs by 20% over three years' makes it clear when performance will be judged **[An]**. This allows managers to monitor progress throughout the period and take corrective action if the business is falling behind **[An]**. Without a time limit, there is no urgency and employees may consistently prioritise short-term tasks at the expense of more important longer-term goals **[An]**

A business should also ensure objectives are realistic and agreed with employees rather than simply imposed on them **[K]**. If targets are perceived as unachievable - for example, demanding a large increase in productivity without providing additional resources or training - employees are likely to become demotivated **[An]**. This can lead to increased absenteeism and higher labour turnover, raising recruitment and training costs while reducing productivity further **[An]**. Objectives that are discussed and mutually agreed are more likely to gain employee commitment, creating a shared sense of purpose and significantly improving the chances that the business achieves what it set out to do **[An]**

parts.problem_md: Analyse the** **ways in which ethics may influence the activities of a business.
parts.solution_md:
One way ethics may influence business activities is through sourcing and supply chain decisions **[K]**. A business committed to ethical behaviour may refuse to use suppliers that employ child labour or pay extremely low wages, even if this would reduce costs significantly **[An]**. While this places the business at a cost disadvantage compared to less scrupulous competitors, it builds a positive reputation with consumers who increasingly choose brands that align with their values **[An]**. Over time, this trust generates greater customer loyalty and protects the business from reputational damage that could prove far more costly than the savings it forfeited **[An]**

Ethics may also influence a business's environmental decisions **[K]**. A business may reject production methods that pollute the environment, such as cheap waste disposal or high-emission processes, and instead invest in more sustainable alternatives **[An]**. This increases short-term operating costs but reduces the risk of legal penalties from regulators and reputational damage from pressure groups or negative media coverage **[An]**. It can also attract ethically minded customers and investors, improving long-term financial performance. In industries where environmental standards are tightening, early adoption of ethical practices can give a business a significant competitive advantage **[An]**

parts.problem_md: Analyse **two **reasons why it is important for a business to set SMART objectives.
parts.solution_md:
One reason SMART objectives are important is that they are measurable **[K]**, meaning a business can track its progress and assess whether it is on course to achieve its goals. Without a measurable target, such as 'increase market share by 5% within 12 months', there is no way of knowing whether the business is succeeding or falling short **[An]**. This allows managers to identify problems early and take corrective action before significant resources are wasted **[An]**. Consistently hitting measurable targets also builds confidence among shareholders and stakeholders, improving the business's ability to attract investment and support over time **[An]**

SMART objectives are also important because they are specific and achievable **[K]**, giving employees a clear sense of direction and realistic targets to work towards. Vague objectives such as 'do better this year' offer no clarity about what employees should prioritise or how success will be defined, leading to wasted effort and inconsistent decision-making **[An]**. Specific objectives focus effort on the activities that matter most. Achievable targets also maintain employee motivation - if targets are set too high, employees may become disengaged and productivity will fall **[An]**. Setting objectives that stretch but do not overwhelm is therefore essential for sustaining long-term business performance **[An]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - SMART objectives are measurable, meaning a business can track its progress and assess whether it is on course to meet its goals. This allows managers to identify problems early and take corrective action before resources are wasted, making it far more likely that the business achieves what it set out to do.
> - SMART objectives are specific, giving employees and managers a clear sense of what needs to be achieved and why. Vague objectives such as 'improve performance' offer no direction, leading to wasted effort and inconsistent priorities. Specificity focuses the whole business on the activities that will deliver results.
> - SMART objectives are time-limited, which creates discipline and ensures that important longer-term goals are not sacrificed for short-term pressures. A deadline also provides a clear point at which performance can be reviewed, making accountability easier to enforce across departments and teams.
> - SMART objectives are achievable and realistic, which helps maintain employee motivation. Targets that are set too high can demoralise employees if they feel success is impossible; targets that are too easy provide no incentive to improve. Objectives that stretch but do not overwhelm employees help sustain productivity and engagement over time.
> - However, an over-reliance on SMART objectives could make a business inflexible and stifle creativity, particularly in fast-changing markets where rigid targets may become outdated before the time limit is reached
